source.title: Probability-Signature Dynamics: Unpacking Modular Addition Learning Within Two-Layer Networks
source.authors: Yun-Jing Wang; Jun-Jie Yao; Lin-Yu Liu; Pin-Yan Lu; Zhi-qin John Xu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some results are shown only in figures.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own clean-versus-noise training dynamics and argues that uniformly random label noise can have faster early loss decrease. It also shows training and test accuracy across label-noise ratios, but those curves are figure-only.
record.gate_note: The cited results from Zhang et al. (2017) and Arpit et al. (2017) are prior work, not this study's results. The paper reports no direct test of shuffled or Gaussian-noise inputs. Values used only in the gradient approximation and its cosine-similarity comparison do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports early clean/noisy-label learning dynamics that qualify V6, and training outcomes showing that weight decay can prevent noisy-label fitting. Its all-random-label and noise-ratio experiments also bear on V1 and V4, although their outcomes cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the label-noise conclusion: conditional label collisions explain faster initial loss decrease on uniformly corrupted examples. The paper's broader conclusion also concerns deriving Fourier and Hadamard representation structure from probability signatures, with an approximation restricted to a particular training regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a two-layer embedding MLP on modular addition with a clean/noise mixture and primarily studies early loss dynamics; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment as described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Early clean/noise loss comparison is reported across α = 0.1–0.9. Accuracy plots also vary optimizer, weight decay, and initialization scale, but the text does not state the corresponding accuracy outcomes across conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix F.1 reports faster early loss decrease for multiplication modulo 60 than modulo 59 or 61.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditional label collisions predict initial loss slopes across structured arithmetic tasks.

record.problems: The main dynamics analysis is an approximation focused on dominant gradient terms and a particular training regime; the authors say it may not remain valid throughout training. Some accuracy results relevant to random labels and noise ratios are figure-only in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted beyond the 60-row limit. Figure 6 has additional combinations of weight decay and initialization scale; they are not separate rows here because those curves provide no stated or recoverable outcome for the versions at issue.

untested.parts: Whether all-random labels yield near-zero training error and chance test performance with the true-label training recipe unchanged cannot be established from the supplied text.
No time-to-fitting comparison or small constant-factor slowdown is reported. Initial loss slopes do not establish convergence time.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
Steady test-error degradation from zero to complete corruption cannot be assessed from the supplied text.

Dropout and data augmentation are not tested. Removing regularization on an entirely true-label training set is not tested; the reported no-weight-decay generalization failure uses corrupted training labels.
The early loss comparison does not directly measure the timing of shared-pattern acquisition relative to accurate noisy-label fitting.

missing.what: Figure 1 explicitly reports clean/noisy training accuracy and test accuracy at α = 0.1 and γ = 0.5: λ = 0 gives 100% clean/noisy training accuracy and 0% test accuracy; λ = 0.0001 gives nearly 100% on all three; λ = 0.0005 forgets noise while generalizing; λ = 0.001 fails to converge. Extract separate condition rows.
ReLU training with 30% noise reaches high accuracy on both clean and noisy examples before decay and later grokking. This directly bears on the ordering of memorization and generalization.

Collision-controlled bijective corruption reverses the early loss ordering with corruption fraction: corrupted examples decrease first below α = 0.5, and clean examples decrease first above α = 0.5. Extract this separately from uniformly random corruption.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source for any listed version. No numerical outcomes were inferred from missing figure curves. The bijective-corruption control changes the early ordering but does not use independent random labels. Poor generalization without weight decay on a corrupted dataset does not challenge V5's separate true-label generalization clause.

versions.untested_parts: The paper includes an all-noise condition in Figure 6, but provides no textual result or recoverable numerical values for training error or test error at that condition.
Accuracy curves across noise ratios are shown in Figure 6, but the text does not state the training and test accuracy outcomes across the full sweep.
The paper compares early loss decrease for clean and noisy examples; it does not establish the full sequence through later memorization across training.

rows.subject: two-layer embedding MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared early loss dynamics for clean and uniformly random label-noise examples.
rows.measure: Relative rate of loss decrease for clean versus noise examples.
rows.value: Noise loss always decreases more rapidly.
rows.note: The authors state that the early faster decrease holds under almost any ratio of noise.
rows.check: Correct for the measured early loss-slope comparison: noisy-example loss decreases faster across α = 0.1–0.9. This does not establish that noisy labels reach accurate fitting before shared clean patterns are learned.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6. Noisy-example loss decreases faster initially, but this comparison does not establish whether shared clean patterns are fitted before noisy labels are memorized.
source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1; Figure 4 caption and noise-ratio panel labels; Appendix A model dimensions.
source_check.problem: The reversed state conflates early loss-decrease rates with the order of pattern acquisition and memorization.

rows.subject: two-layer embedding MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with uniformly random labels at α = 1; accuracy curves are shown.
rows.note: The supplied text identifies the plotted conditions, but gives no prose result or recoverable values for α = 1.
rows.check: The all-random-label condition also bears on weight decay's ability to prevent fitting, but Figure 6's outcomes are unreadable in the supplied text. Split the initialization and weight-decay settings into separate rows when outcomes are available.

rows.subject: two-layer embedding MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained across label-noise ratios; accuracy curves are shown.
rows.note: Curves are plotted for these settings, but the prose does not describe their accuracy outcomes across noise ratios.
rows.check: The supplied text does not recover the accuracy outcomes. Separate noise ratios and training settings; α = 1 overlaps R2. The plotted sweep does not include the no-noise endpoint required for the full V4 trajectory.

relationships.condition: GELU modular-addition MLP, uniformly random label corruption α = 0.1–0.9, first 100 epochs
relationships.reason: R1 reports faster noisy-example loss decrease, qualifying a clean-first interpretation of initial learning speed; loss slopes alone do not establish the order of pattern acquisition and memorization.
relationships.display_finding: Noisy-example losses decreased faster initially, but loss slopes alone did not establish the order of shared-pattern learning and noisy-label memorization.
